extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students in philosophy of mathematics, proof theory, and mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating purity and explanation of proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic analysis of criteria and models used to assess when a mathematical proof is 'pure' or 'explanatory', illustrated by case studies (a proof of Pythagoras’s Theorem and Euclid’s proof of the infinitude of primes). The paper examines existing models (topic, ontology, grounding, complexity/generality, etc.) and how they apply to informal and formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity as an ideal of proof/method: proofs should use methods and objects that are 'pure' with respect to the theorem (e.g., not mixing domains unnecessarily); often associated with the literature on purity of methods (Arana & Detlefsen, Pillay, Thorstad, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to evaluate Euclid’s proof of the infinitude of primes as a canonical example of a 'pure' proof. Purity assessments depend on what counts as relevant objects/methods for the theorem (e.g., plane-geometry objects vs arithmetic objects). See Arana (2017, 2022), Arana & Detlefsen (2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory status / explanatory proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proof is explanatory: does it reveal objective reasons or the right sort of explanation for why the theorem holds (e.g., Pythagoras proof considered explanatory)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper applies well-known models of explanation to proofs (references to Steiner, Kitcher, D'Alessandro, Mancosu, Lange). Explanatory criteria include revealing reasons, unification, and showing why a conclusion follows in an illuminating way. Discussion includes how some modern approaches separate explanation from purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontology / ontological purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proof and the theorem commit to a particular ontology (the kinds of objects it quantifies over) and whether that ontology is appropriate/pure with respect to the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Martinot (2024) notion of ontological purity is discussed; example: formalizing Pythagoras arithmetically versus geometrically affects purity (similarity becomes harmless once theorem is formalized arithmetically). Differences in ontological commitments can change purity assessments (plane vs arithmetic ontology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic determination (topic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of the 'topic' of a proof/theorem as used in purity analyses: which subject-matter or objects count as the relevant topic for determining purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arana & Detlefsen’s notion of topic can be sensitive to the precise wording of a theorem and is treated 'naively' in some discussions to match mathematical practice. The paper notes that topic determination can be agent-dependent and this affects purity judgements (see Sect. 3.1 and Arana (2022)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proof generalises to produce new theorems or variants (e.g., changing definitions to get 'prime*' leading to new theorems); generalisability as a marker of explanatory power or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proof's method naturally yields a family of related results, it may be judged explanatory or valuable. The paper discusses that induction, when it is a characterising property, can allow such generalisability (see Hafner & Mancosu (2005) example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity versus generality (simplicity/complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity and generality are often linked (the paper notes they are 'inversely proportional'): simpler proofs may be less general and vice versa; simplicity is a recurring evaluative dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cites Ginammi et al. (2020) and Poggiolesi (2024) on the relation between complexity and generality. Also references debates on simplicity/beauty (Iemhoff, Inglis & Aberdein, Lehet) and how simplicity interacts with purity and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary ontological purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A refined notion of purity (labelled 'secondary ontological purity') proposed by Martinot (2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as an exception to standard purity notions; the paper flags this as a distinct variant of ontological purity without full exposition here (see Martinot (2024)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterising properties of a proof (e.g., induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether certain methods or properties (like induction) are characterising features for a proof, i.e., essential to its method and explanatory role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a property is characterising (e.g., induction), it may affect whether the proof satisfies generalisability or explanatory criteria. The paper notes that when induction would have been characterising for a proof of infinitude of primes, it could have satisfied generalisability similarly to other proofs (Hafner & Mancosu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of grounds/elements to the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that the grounds (reasons) or the content of a proof should not contain elements unrelated to the conclusion; a notion used in grounding-based analyses of explanation and purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats 'grounds do not contain any element that is not related to the conclusion' and 'proof does not contain any element that is not related to the conclusion' as effectively equivalent in the simple examples considered (citing Poggiolesi 2021, 2024). This is used to assess impurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal versus informal proofs and applicability of models
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between purity/explanation analyses for formal (natural deduction/formal proofs) versus informal proofs as written by working mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Martinot’s paper considers purity of natural deduction proofs, this paper focuses on discussion of 'informal' proofs; some purity/explanation models are more directly applicable to one or the other, so choice of proof-format affects evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming axioms into rules and methodological trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological practice in proof theory where axioms are transformed into rules may affect how a proof's purity is judged (use of theorems as rules alters what counts as method/content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Marin et al. (2022) as example of this trend; notes that such transformations can change whether certain features are viewed as part of the method (thus impacting purity assessments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding and Bolzano’s theory of ground/consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Using grounding (Bolzano's theory of ground and consequence) as a framework: explanatory proofs are those that exhibit grounding relations or objective reasons for the theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References Bolzano (Theory of Science) and related literature (Betti, Centrone, Rumberg). The paper uses grounding-theoretic ideas to analyse explanation in mathematical proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic/ontology sensitivity to theorem wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The observation that small changes in theorem wording (e.g., formulation chosen) can affect outcome in explanation and especially purity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes that the precise wording can affect notions like 'topic' (Arana & Detlefsen) and 'ontology' (Martinot 2024), and where this arises the authors aim to objectively discuss different formulations and their potential differences in results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability / operational views of purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Views that treat purity operationally or via interpretability/operational criteria (e.g., what operations/methods are used and how they operate across contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned via Kahle & Pulcini (2017) 'Towards an operational view of purity' and related work; suggests alternative frameworks for assessing purity beyond ontological/topic analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to negation and logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper notes that evaluations can be more complicated in the presence of negated sentences and depend on logical form of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Poggiolesi (2021) for complications arising with negated sentences; implies that logical form can affect both purity and explanatory judgements.
